prize_parts.citation: For the invention and development of optical lattice clocks, bringing frequency and time measurement to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks fit the 'discovery or invention' criterion cleanly. Katori's magic-wavelength proposal removed the lattice light shift while keeping the statistics of many atoms in parallel, and Ye's group carried the strontium clock to record systematic uncertainty and stability. The result is reproduced by several independent laboratories, and it already underpins tests of fundamental constants, relativistic geodesy, dark-matter searches and the expected redefinition of the second. The credit is a clean two-person split between concept and first realisation on one side and performance at the frontier on the other, which is rare among this year's candidates. Four of eight members placed it first in the openings, and I do not treat that as merit in itself, but the independent scientific arguments for it are strong.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is overlap with earlier prizes: frequency combs (2005) and ion-based quantum control and clocks (2012) already honoured much of the surrounding toolkit, so some will read the lattice clock as an incremental step in a recognised lineage. Priority among lattice-clock groups (Yb, Hg and European laboratories) is also not fully settled by the supplied names, and the SI second has not yet been redefined, though that is a policy step rather than a doubt about the physics.

responses.point: Pearce ranks B015 first as an instrument-driven advance with a natural two-person credit, and places IceCube (B040, Halzen) second.
responses.response: I agree on B015 and on the credit. On B040 I am more reserved. A single credited name for a very large collaboration does not give a fair configuration, and the identification of individual sources is still at modest significance. I would not combine it with the clock prize, since the two-person clock credit already fills most of the allowed three places.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks magic-angle graphene (B017) first as a sharp prediction plus a decisive experiment, and ranks the lattice clock only seventh.
responses.response: I take B017 seriously, and it is my own second choice. I disagree with ranking the clock seventh, though. The clock is not a smaller discovery, it is a mature and reproduced one. B017 has an unresolved superconducting mechanism, and its credit list leaves out Yuan Cao and other early experimentalists, so the attribution is harder to defend today. That is why I put the clock ahead for this year, while holding B017 as the most likely next candidate.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED (B012) first, noting that it is the architecture behind essentially every superconducting processor, while disclosing Chalmers proximity and the recent 2025 prize.
responses.response: The architectural importance is real, and I appreciate the disclosure given that we share an institution. My qualification is the recency of the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits, which makes a second superconducting-circuit award this soon harder to justify. The four-name credit for B012 also exceeds the limit of three, so one of Blais, Wallraff, Schoelkopf or Girvin would have to be dropped, and the case for dropping any of them is not obvious.

responses.point: Kroll supports B015 with Katori and Ye and ranks Bennett-Brassard (B010) second, while questioning distinctness from the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
responses.response: I share your worry about distinctness from 2005 and 2012, and I think it is answered by the magic-wavelength lattice being a different architecture with many-atom parallelism, not a repeat of ion-clock control. On B010, I agree that the Ekert allocation is unresolved and that the duplicated name entry needs care, but I would not move it ahead of the clock or B017.

uncertainties: Whether the committee judges the lattice clock sufficiently distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes.
How to treat priority among competing lattice-clock groups beyond the two credited names.
Whether B017 would be preferred this year if the experimental credit beyond Jarillo-Herrero is clarified.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B015 or the credited names Katori and Ye. I share Chalmers with Göran Johansson, whose first-ranked candidate is circuit QED (B012), so I would recuse myself or at least flag a conflict if Chalmers colleagues were named in that candidate. My long-running exchanges with Japanese universities are general and do not involve the candidates.
